'''willy-nilly''' (wil′i-nil′i), ''a.'' or ''adv.'' '''1.''' Will he or will he not; will ye or will ye not; willing or unwilling. See ''nill''<sup>1</sup>, ''will''<sup>2</sup>.—'''2.''' Vacillating; shilly-shallying.

{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 295.}}}}
'''2.''' To receive willingly; consent or submit to.

¶
'''Wilson’s thrush.''' See ''veery'' (with cut).

'''wilt<sup>1</sup>''' (wilt), ''v.'' [Also ''welt'', dial. variants of ''wilk'', ''welk'' (= G. ''welk'', withered, ''verwelken'', fade, wither): see ''welk''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To droop or fade, as plants or flowers when cut or plucked; wither.
{{smaller block|To ''wilt'', for wither, spoken of green herbs or flowers, is a general word.
{{right|''Ray.''}}
The frosts have fallen and the flowers are drooping, summer ''wilts'' into autumn.
{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, ii. 5.}}}}
'''2.''' To become soft or languid; lose energy, pith, or strength. [Colloq., U. S.]

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To cause to droop or become languid, as a plant; take the stiffness, strength, or vigor out of; hence, to render limp and pithless; depress.
{{smaller block|Despots have ''wilted'' the human race into sloth and imbecility.
{{right|''Dwight.''}}
She wanted a pink that Miss Amy had pinned on her breast . . . and died, holding the ''wilted'' stem in her hand.
{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, ii. 1.}}}}

'''wilt<sup>2</sup>''' (wilt). The second person singular present indicative of ''will''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Wilton carpet.''' See ''carpet.''

'''wiluite''' (wil′ụ̄-īt), ''n.'' [< ''Wilui'' (see def.) + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' A variety of grossular garnet from the Wilui (Vilui) river in eastern Siberia.—'''2.''' A variety of vesuvianite from the same locality.

Also ''viluite.''

'''wily''' (wī′li), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''wilie'', ''wylie''; < ME. ''wily'', ''wyly''; < ''wile''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Full of wiles; subtle; cunning; crafty; sly.
